The following text is based on a real news article published in 2019 by Warren Cornwall in Science [1].

 

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. (For the record, from  1970 to 2019, the global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius.)  

Where Were the Models Off?

A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades. 

It turns out it’s incredibly difficult to predict our future pollution. For example, some models from the 1980s that initially looked "too warm" didn't factor in a steep, unexpected drop in planet-warming refrigerants, resulting from the success of the 1989 Montreal Protocol to repair the ozone layer. They also sometimes overestimated the release of other gases, such as methane.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

Sources:  

[1] Original article: Cornwall, W. (2019) Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming. Science. Link: https://www.science.org/content/article/even-50-year-old-climate-models-correctly-predicted-global-warming

[2] Hausfather, Z., Drake, H. F., Abbott, T., & Schmidt, G. A. (2020). Evaluating the Performance of Past Climate Model Projections. Geophysical Research Letters. Link: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2019GL085378

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

The following text is based on a real news article published in 2019 by Warren Cornwall in Science [1].

 

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. (For the record, from  1970 to 2019, the global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius.)  

Where Were the Models Off?

A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades. 

It turns out it’s incredibly difficult to predict our future pollution. For example, some models from the 1980s that initially looked "too warm" didn't factor in a steep, unexpected drop in planet-warming refrigerants, resulting from the success of the 1989 Montreal Protocol to repair the ozone layer. They also sometimes overestimated the release of other gases, such as methane.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

Sources:  

[1] Original article: Cornwall, W. (2019) Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming. Science. Link: https://www.science.org/content/article/even-50-year-old-climate-models-correctly-predicted-global-warming

[2] Hausfather, Z., Drake, H. F., Abbott, T., & Schmidt, G. A. (2020). Evaluating the Performance of Past Climate Model Projections. Geophysical Research Letters. Link: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2019GL085378

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. (For the record, from  1970 to 2019, the global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius.)  

Where Were the Models Off?

A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades. 

It turns out it’s incredibly difficult to predict our future pollution. They also sometimes overestimated the release of other gases, such as methane.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

The following text is based on a real news article published in 2019 by Warren Cornwall in Science [1].

 

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. (For the record, from  1970 to 2019, the global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius.)  

Where Were the Models Off?

A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades. 

It turns out it’s incredibly difficult to predict our future pollution. For example, some models from the 1980s that initially looked "too warm" didn't factor in a steep, unexpected drop in planet-warming refrigerants, resulting from the success of the 1989 Montreal Protocol to repair the ozone layer. They also sometimes overestimated the release of other gases, such as methane.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

The following text is based on a real news article published in 2019 by Warren Cornwall in Science [1].

 

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. (For the record, from  1970 to 2019, the global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius.)  

Where Were the Models Off?

A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades. 

It turns out it’s incredibly difficult to predict our future pollution. For example, some models from the 1980s that initially looked "too warm" didn't factor in a steep, unexpected drop in planet-warming refrigerants, resulting from the success of the 1989 Montreal Protocol to repair the ozone layer. They also sometimes overestimated the release of other gases, such as methane.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

Sources:

The following text is based on a real news article published in 2019 by Warren Cornwall in Science [1].

 

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. (For the record, from  1970 to 2019, the global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius.)  

Where Were the Models Off?

A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades. 

It turns out it’s incredibly difficult to predict our future pollution. For example, some models from the 1980s that initially looked "too warm" didn't factor in a steep, unexpected drop in planet-warming refrigerants, resulting from the success of the 1989 Montreal Protocol to repair the ozone layer. They also sometimes overestimated the release of other gases, such as methane.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. gender: Female.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

The following text is based on a real news article published in 2019 by Warren Cornwall in Science [1].

 

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. (For the record, from  1970 to 2019, the global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius.)  

Where Were the Models Off?

A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades. 

It turns out it’s incredibly difficult to predict our future pollution. For example, some models from the 1980s that initially looked "too warm" didn't factor in a steep, unexpected drop in planet-warming refrigerants, resulting from the success of the 1989 Montreal Protocol to repair the ozone layer. They also sometimes overestimated the release of other gases, such as methane.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

Sources:  

[1] Original article: Cornwall, W. (2019) Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming. Science. Link: https://www.science.org/content/article/even-50-year-old-climate-models-correctly-predicted-global-warming

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

The following text is based on a real news article published in 2019 by Warren Cornwall in Science [1].

 

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. (For the record, from  1970 to 2019, the global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius.)  

Where Were the Models Off?

A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades. 

It turns out it’s incredibly difficult to predict our future pollution. For example, some models from the 1980s that initially looked "too warm" didn't factor in a steep, unexpected drop in planet-warming refrigerants, resulting from the success of the 1989 Montreal Protocol to repair the ozone layer. They also sometimes overestimated the release of other gases, such as methane.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

Sources:

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

The following text is based on a real news article published in 2019 by Warren Cornwall in Science [1].

 

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. (For the record, from  1970 to 2019, the global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius.)  

Where Were the Models Off?

A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades. 

It turns out it’s incredibly difficult to predict our future pollution. For example, some models from the 1980s that initially looked "too warm" didn't factor in a steep, unexpected drop in planet-warming refrigerants, resulting from the success of the 1989 Montreal Protocol to repair the ozone layer. They also sometimes overestimated the release of other gases, such as methane.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

Sources:  

[1] Original article: Cornwall, W. (2019) Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming. Science. Link: https://www.science.org/content/article/even-50-year-old-climate-models-correctly-predicted-global-warming

Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. income: $56,000 to $99,999.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

The following text is based on a real news article published in 2019 by Warren Cornwall in Science [1].

 

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. (For the record, from  1970 to 2019, the global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius.)  

Where Were the Models Off?

A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades. 

It turns out it’s incredibly difficult to predict our future pollution. For example, some models from the 1980s that initially looked "too warm" didn't factor in a steep, unexpected drop in planet-warming refrigerants, resulting from the success of the 1989 Montreal Protocol to repair the ozone layer. They also sometimes overestimated the release of other gases, such as methane.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

Sources:  

[1] Original article: Cornwall, W. (2019) Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming. Science. Link: https://www.science.org/content/article/even-50-year-old-climate-models-correctly-predicted-global-warming

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

The following text is based on a real news article published in 2019 by Warren Cornwall in Science [1].

 

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. (For the record, from  1970 to 2019, the global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius.)  

Where Were the Models Off?

A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades. 

It turns out it’s incredibly difficult to predict our future pollution. For example, some models from the 1980s that initially looked "too warm" didn't factor in a steep, unexpected drop in planet-warming refrigerants, resulting from the success of the 1989 Montreal Protocol to repair the ozone layer. They also sometimes overestimated the release of other gases, such as methane.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

Sources:  

[1] Original article: Cornwall, W. (2019) Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming. Science. Link: https://www.science.org/content/article/even-50-year-old-climate-models-correctly-predicted-global-warming

[2] Hausfather, Z., Drake, H. F., Abbott, T., & Schmidt, G. A. (2020). Evaluating the Performance of Past Climate Model Projections. Geophysical Research Letters. Link: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2019GL085378

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. (For the record, from  1970 to 2019, the global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius.)  

Where Were the Models Off?

A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades. 

It turns out it’s incredibly difficult to predict our future pollution. For example, some models from the 1980s that initially looked "too warm" didn't factor in a steep, unexpected drop in planet-warming refrigerants, resulting from the success of the 1989 Montreal Protocol to repair the ozone layer. They also sometimes overestimated the release of other gases, such as methane.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. (For the record, from  1970 to 2019, the global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius.)  

Where Were the Models Off?

A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades. 

It turns out it’s incredibly difficult to predict our future pollution. For example, some models from the 1980s that initially looked "too warm" didn't factor in a steep, unexpected drop in planet-warming refrigerants, resulting from the success of the 1989 Montreal Protocol to repair the ozone layer. They also sometimes overestimated the release of other gases, such as methane.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

Even 50-year-old climate models correctly predicted global warming

You may have heard the criticism that climate scientists build computer models that can’t predict the future. But decades later, those predictions turned out to be strikingly accurate.

Climate scientists first began using computers to predict global temperatures in the 1970s. The early models were simple compared to what today's supercomputers produce, but a recent extensive review of 17 known forecasts made between 1970 and 2001 found that most of them were remarkably accurate [2]. All of them got the direction of change right, and most of them got the amount of change right, within a small margin of error. A few models did predict warming that was slightly too high or too low—by up to 0.1 degrees per decade. These small errors were mostly due to incorrect predictions about human behavior, not a flaw in the fundamental physics of the models.

Climate models require two main inputs: First, physics—how the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and land behave; Second, human actions—how much pollution (greenhouse gases like CO2 but also cooling aerosols, like soot) humans will emit into the atmosphere over the decades.

When researchers adjusted these older models to use the actual historical pollution levels (instead of the levels they originally guessed), the predictions from those models lined up almost perfectly with the temperatures we observe today.

The Bottom Line

Climate models are not perfect, and they can’t predict everything. But the half-century of modelling history provides strong evidence both that the fundamental science used by climate scientists is broadly correct, and that models built upon that science to  project future warming have been largely correct as well.

Oil companies knew.

By 1959–more than 60 years ago–they knew that burning fossil fuels could lead to global warming “sufficient to melt the icecap and submerge New York.” During the 1970s and ‘80s, scientists at one oil giant predicted global warming with breathtaking accuracy and warned executives of “potentially catastrophic” climate effects. 

Oil companies lied.

Starting in the late 1980s, oil companies spent the next two decades intentionally misleading the American public with a well-funded disinformation campaign intended to create doubt about climate science and generate mistrust in climate scientists.

Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. age_band: 45-59.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Some people think that climate scientists cannot be trusted. You’d be forgiven for feeling that way, because the fossil fuel industry has bankrolled a multi-decade propaganda campaign specifically designed to stop action on climate change by undermining the public’s trust in climate science and scientists. Initially, in the 1970s and early 1980s, oil companies agreed with academic and federal scientists that burning fossil fuels would lead to climate change; some companies even employed their own climate scientists and conducted in-house climate science research. But as the public and politicians began to wake up to the climate crisis in the early 1990s, instead of alerting the public or taking action, the fossil fuel industry began to attack climate science and scientists. Trust the climate scientists, don’t let oil companies mislead you.

Here are some more details:

Oil companies knew.

Over the past decade, historians and journalists have discovered internal memos from oil companies showing that the oil industry has known since the 1950s that their products could cause dangerous climate change. Oil companies employed and worked with some of the world’s top climate scientists. By 1959–more than 60 years ago–they knew that burning fossil fuels could lead to global warming “sufficient to melt the icecap and submerge New York.” During the 1970s and ‘80s, scientists at one oil giant predicted global warming with breathtaking accuracy and warned executives of “potentially catastrophic” climate effects. 

Oil companies lied.

Starting in the late 1980s, oil companies spent the next two decades intentionally misleading the American public with a well-funded disinformation campaign intended to create doubt about climate science and generate mistrust in climate scientists.  

The result was a manufactured debate about climate change that undermined public understanding of the scientific consensus that climate change is real and human-caused. The fossil fuel industry’s internal memos made this propaganda strategy explicit: “Emphasize the uncertainty” in climate science and “Reposition global warming as theory (not fact).” Their goal was to confuse the public and policymakers in order to delay action and protect profits.

As part of this attack on the scientific consensus, oil companies issued statements and advertisements falsely claiming that climate science was “unsettled.” They also funded a small but vocal group of contrarian scientists and fake experts to sustain the illusion that there was significant disagreement within the scientific community. From 1986 to 2015, five oil companies alone spent $3.6 billion on advertising. Money also went to lobbying politicians against climate change legislation - outspending environmental groups by 10-to-1.

Oil companies harassed.

Climate scientists themselves also became the victims of an orchestrated smear campaign. For example, when one world-renowned climate scientist, Dr. Benjamin Santer, coauthored a major report concluding that human-caused global warming was underway, he was publicly accused of fraud and corruption by an oil-industry front group.Despite these claims being false and baseless, Dr. Santer faced harassment and threatening emails. 

When another prominent climate scientist, Dr. Michael Mann, coauthored research demonstrating rapid global warming over the past century, he was harassed for years by bogus legal complaints filed by organizations funded by fossil fuel interests. Fossil fuel companies used these attacks to misportray climate scientists as untrustworthy and convince the public not to believe their work.

When it comes to climate change, don’t trust the oil companies, trust the climate scientists.

Sources:

Cook, J., Supran, G., Lewandowsky, S., Oreskes, N., & Maibach, E. (2019). America misled: How the fossil fuel industry deliberately misled Americans about climate change. George Mason University Center for Climate Change Communication. https://www.climatechangecommunication.org/america-misled/

Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. education: Bachelor's degree.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Some people think that climate scientists cannot be trusted. You’d be forgiven for feeling that way, because the fossil fuel industry has bankrolled a multi-decade propaganda campaign specifically designed to stop action on climate change by undermining the public’s trust in climate science and scientists. Initially, in the 1970s and early 1980s, oil companies agreed with academic and federal scientists that burning fossil fuels would lead to climate change; some companies even employed their own climate scientists and conducted in-house climate science research. But as the public and politicians began to wake up to the climate crisis in the early 1990s, instead of alerting the public or taking action, the fossil fuel industry began to attack climate science and scientists. Trust the climate scientists, don’t let oil companies mislead you.

Here are some more details:

Oil companies knew.

Over the past decade, historians and journalists have discovered internal memos from oil companies showing that the oil industry has known since the 1950s that their products could cause dangerous climate change. Oil companies employed and worked with some of the world’s top climate scientists. By 1959–more than 60 years ago–they knew that burning fossil fuels could lead to global warming “sufficient to melt the icecap and submerge New York.” During the 1970s and ‘80s, scientists at one oil giant predicted global warming with breathtaking accuracy and warned executives of “potentially catastrophic” climate effects. 

Oil companies lied.

Starting in the late 1980s, oil companies spent the next two decades intentionally misleading the American public with a well-funded disinformation campaign intended to create doubt about climate science and generate mistrust in climate scientists.  

The result was a manufactured debate about climate change that undermined public understanding of the scientific consensus that climate change is real and human-caused. The fossil fuel industry’s internal memos made this propaganda strategy explicit: “Emphasize the uncertainty” in climate science and “Reposition global warming as theory (not fact).” Their goal was to confuse the public and policymakers in order to delay action and protect profits.

As part of this attack on the scientific consensus, oil companies issued statements and advertisements falsely claiming that climate science was “unsettled.” They also funded a small but vocal group of contrarian scientists and fake experts to sustain the illusion that there was significant disagreement within the scientific community. From 1986 to 2015, five oil companies alone spent $3.6 billion on advertising. Money also went to lobbying politicians against climate change legislation - outspending environmental groups by 10-to-1.

Oil companies harassed.

Climate scientists themselves also became the victims of an orchestrated smear campaign. For example, when one world-renowned climate scientist, Dr. Benjamin Santer, coauthored a major report concluding that human-caused global warming was underway, he was publicly accused of fraud and corruption by an oil-industry front group.Despite these claims being false and baseless, Dr. Santer faced harassment and threatening emails. 

When another prominent climate scientist, Dr. Michael Mann, coauthored research demonstrating rapid global warming over the past century, he was harassed for years by bogus legal complaints filed by organizations funded by fossil fuel interests. Fossil fuel companies used these attacks to misportray climate scientists as untrustworthy and convince the public not to believe their work.

When it comes to climate change, don’t trust the oil companies, trust the climate scientists.

Sources:

Brulle, R.J., Aronczyk, M. & Carmichael, J. (2020). Corporate promotion and climate change: an analysis of key variables affecting advertising spending by major oil corporations, 1986–2015. Climatic Change, 159, 87–101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-019-02582-8

Cook, J., Supran, G., Lewandowsky, S., Oreskes, N., & Maibach, E. (2019). America misled: How the fossil fuel industry deliberately misled Americans about climate change. George Mason University Center for Climate Change Communication. https://www.climatechangecommunication.org/america-misled/
Oreskes, N., & Conway, E. M. (2011). Merchants of doubt: How a handful of scientists obscured the truth on issues from tobacco smoke to global warming. Bloomsbury Publishing USA.

Supran, G., & Oreskes, N. (2017). Assessing ExxonMobil’s climate change communications (1977–2014). Environmental Research Letters, 12, 084019. https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aa815f
Union of Concerned Scientists. (2017, October 12). How the fossil fuel industry harassed climate scientist Michael Mann. https://www.ucs.org/resources/how-fossil-fuel-industry-harassed-climate-scientist-michael-mann

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Some people think that climate scientists cannot be trusted. You’d be forgiven for feeling that way, because the fossil fuel industry has bankrolled a multi-decade propaganda campaign specifically designed to stop action on climate change by undermining the public’s trust in climate science and scientists. Initially, in the 1970s and early 1980s, oil companies agreed with academic and federal scientists that burning fossil fuels would lead to climate change; some companies even employed their own climate scientists and conducted in-house climate science research. But as the public and politicians began to wake up to the climate crisis in the early 1990s, instead of alerting the public or taking action, the fossil fuel industry began to attack climate science and scientists. Trust the climate scientists, don’t let oil companies mislead you.

Here are some more details:

Oil companies knew.

Over the past decade, historians and journalists have discovered internal memos from oil companies showing that the oil industry has known since the 1950s that their products could cause dangerous climate change. Oil companies employed and worked with some of the world’s top climate scientists. By 1959–more than 60 years ago–they knew that burning fossil fuels could lead to global warming “sufficient to melt the icecap and submerge New York.” During the 1970s and ‘80s, scientists at one oil giant predicted global warming with breathtaking accuracy and warned executives of “potentially catastrophic” climate effects. 

Oil companies lied.

Starting in the late 1980s, oil companies spent the next two decades intentionally misleading the American public with a well-funded disinformation campaign intended to create doubt about climate science and generate mistrust in climate scientists.  

The result was a manufactured debate about climate change that undermined public understanding of the scientific consensus that climate change is real and human-caused. The fossil fuel industry’s internal memos made this propaganda strategy explicit: “Emphasize the uncertainty” in climate science and “Reposition global warming as theory (not fact).” Their goal was to confuse the public and policymakers in order to delay action and protect profits.

As part of this attack on the scientific consensus, oil companies issued statements and advertisements falsely claiming that climate science was “unsettled.” They also funded a small but vocal group of contrarian scientists and fake experts to sustain the illusion that there was significant disagreement within the scientific community. From 1986 to 2015, five oil companies alone spent $3.6 billion on advertising. Money also went to lobbying politicians against climate change legislation - outspending environmental groups by 10-to-1.

Oil companies harassed.

Climate scientists themselves also became the victims of an orchestrated smear campaign. For example, when one world-renowned climate scientist, Dr. Benjamin Santer, coauthored a major report concluding that human-caused global warming was underway, he was publicly accused of fraud and corruption by an oil-industry front group.Despite these claims being false and baseless, Dr. Santer faced harassment and threatening emails. 

When another prominent climate scientist, Dr. Michael Mann, coauthored research demonstrating rapid global warming over the past century, he was harassed for years by bogus legal complaints filed by organizations funded by fossil fuel interests. Fossil fuel companies used these attacks to misportray climate scientists as untrustworthy and convince the public not to believe their work.

When it comes to climate change, don’t trust the oil companies, trust the climate scientists.

Thinking Process:

1.  **Analyze the Demographic:** The demographic is defined by having a "High school diploma / GED." This represents a group with a foundational level of education, which might predispose them to believe in scientific consensus but might also correlate with lower political trust or less engagement with complex scientific narratives compared to highly educated groups.

    *   Accuse the fossil fuel industry of lying.
    *   Attribute deliberate misinformation campaigns to oil companies (manufactured doubt).
    *   Frame climate scientists as trustworthy heroes who are being harassed and attacked by corporate interests.
    *   The explicit message is: "Don’t trust the oil companies, trust the climate scientists."

3.  **Determine the Impact of the Prompt:** This priming is designed to *increase* trust in climate scientists and *increase* support for climate action among participants. Given the strong framing, the predicted mean answers should skew toward higher scores (more trust, more concern, more support).

4.  **Predict Mean Answers by Question Category:**

    *   **Trust in Climate Scientists (Competence, Integrity, Benevolence, Openness):** The prompt is extremely strong in validating the integrity and competence of scientists while villainizing corporate actors. Therefore, trust scores should be high.
        *   *Competence/Intelligence/Qualification:* High (80-90 range).
        *   *Integrity/Ethical/Sincere:* Very High (85-95 range, especially integrity, given the industry critique).
        *   *Benevolence:* High (75-85 range).
        *   *Openness:* High (75-85 range).
        *   *Overall Trust/Distrust:* High trust (>75), Low distrust (<25).

    *   **Belief/Knowledge (belief_post):** The prompt establishes that climate change is real and human-caused, and that the industry is lying about this. Belief in the core premise should be very high. (85-95).

    *   **Ancillary Trust (EPA, NASA, etc.):** Since the prompt emphasizes that science (backed by scientists) is true and the industry is deceptive, trust in established scientific bodies (NASA, NOAA, universities) tends to be high, even if general trust in the *Federal Government* remains moderate.

    *   **Policy/Action (policy_general, policy_specific_X):** The priming is explicitly an appeal for action against fossil fuel interests. Support for climate action, regulation, and green transitions should be high among this group.
        *   *Policy General:* Strongly supportive (75-90).
        *   *Specific Policies (Taxes, Green Energy, Land Protection):* Strongly supportive (70-90).

    *   **Behavioral Intentions (behavior_X):** High concern and high belief translate into high intentions. They are more likely to engage in climate-friendly behaviors. (65-85 range).

    *   **Funding/Donation (funding_perceptions, donation_ams):** Because of the framing (corporate lies, urgent crisis), public demand for research funding increases. High likelihood of donating.

5.  **Refining Scores (Applying the High School Diploma/GED context):** While the priming is powerful, respondents with only a high school education might have slightly lower scores on extremely technical or nuanced policy issues compared to PhDs, but they will strongly align with the moral message of "trust the scientists." The scores should be high, reflecting the powerful framing effect.

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Some people think that climate scientists cannot be trusted. You’d be forgiven for feeling that way, because the fossil fuel industry has bankrolled a multi-decade propaganda campaign specifically designed to stop action on climate change by undermining the public’s trust in climate science and scientists. Initially, in the 1970s and early 1980s, oil companies agreed with academic and federal scientists that burning fossil fuels would lead to climate change; some companies even employed their own climate scientists and conducted in-house climate science research. But as the public and politicians began to wake up to the climate crisis in the early 1990s, instead of alerting the public or taking action, the fossil fuel industry began to attack climate science and scientists. Trust the climate scientists, don’t let oil companies mislead you.

Here are some more details:

Oil companies knew.

Over the past decade, historians and journalists have discovered internal memos from oil companies showing that the oil industry has known since the 1950s that their products could cause dangerous climate change. Oil companies employed and worked with some of the world’s top climate scientists. By 1959–more than 60 years ago–they knew that burning fossil fuels could lead to global warming “sufficient to melt the icecap and submerge New York.” During the 1970s and ‘80s, scientists at one oil giant predicted global warming with breathtaking accuracy and warned executives of “potentially catastrophic” climate effects. 

Oil companies lied.

Starting in the late 1980s, oil companies spent the next two decades intentionally misleading the American public with a well-funded disinformation campaign intended to create doubt about climate science and generate mistrust in climate scientists.  

The result was a manufactured debate about climate change that undermined public understanding of the scientific consensus that climate change is real and human-caused. The fossil fuel industry’s internal memos made this propaganda strategy explicit: “Emphasize the uncertainty” in climate science and “Reposition global warming as theory (not fact).” Their goal was to confuse the public and policymakers in order to delay action and protect profits.

As part of this attack on the scientific consensus, oil companies issued statements and advertisements falsely claiming that climate science was “unsettled.” They also funded a small but vocal group of contrarian scientists and fake experts to sustain the illusion that there was significant disagreement within the scientific community. From 1986 to 2015, five oil companies alone spent $3.6 billion on advertising. Money also went to lobbying politicians against climate change legislation - outspending environmental groups by 10-to-1.

Oil companies harassed.

Climate scientists themselves also became the victims of an orchestrated smear campaign. For example, when one world-renowned climate scientist, Dr. Benjamin Santer, coauthored a major report concluding that human-caused global warming was underway, he was publicly accused of fraud and corruption by an oil-industry front group.Despite these claims being false and baseless, Dr. Santer faced harassment and threatening emails. 

When another prominent climate scientist, Dr. Michael Mann, coauthored research demonstrating rapid global warming over the past century, he was harassed for years by bogus legal complaints filed by organizations funded by fossil fuel interests. Fossil fuel companies used these attacks to misportray climate scientists as untrustworthy and convince the public not to believe their work.

When it comes to climate change, don’t trust the oil companies, trust the climate scientists.

Oreskes, N., & Conway, E. M. (2011). Merchants of doubt: How a handful of scientists obscured the truth on issues from tobacco smoke to global warming. Bloomsbury Publishing USA.

Supran, G., & Oreskes, N. (2017). Assessing ExxonMobil’s climate change communications (1977–2014). Environmental Research Letters, 12, 084019. https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aa815f
Union of Concerned Scientists. (2017, October 12). How the fossil fuel industry harassed climate scientist Michael Mann. https://www.ucs.org/resources/how-fossil-fuel-industry-harassed-climate-scientist-michael-mann

records.question:
Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. gender: Female.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Some people think that climate scientists cannot be trusted. You’d be forgiven for feeling that way, because the fossil fuel industry has bankrolled a multi-decade propaganda campaign specifically designed to stop action on climate change by undermining the public’s trust in climate science and scientists. Initially, in the 1970s and early 1980s, oil companies agreed with academic and federal scientists that burning fossil fuels would lead to climate change; some companies even employed their own climate scientists and conducted in-house climate science research. But as the public and politicians began to wake up to the climate crisis in the early 1990s, instead of alerting the public or taking action, the fossil fuel industry began to attack climate science and scientists. Trust the climate scientists, don’t let oil companies mislead you.

Here are some more details:

Oil companies knew.

Over the past decade, historians and journalists have discovered internal memos from oil companies showing that the oil industry has known since the 1950s that their products could cause dangerous climate change. Oil companies employed and worked with some of the world’s top climate scientists. By 1959–more than 60 years ago–they knew that burning fossil fuels could lead to global warming “sufficient to melt the icecap and submerge New York.” During the 1970s and ‘80s, scientists at one oil giant predicted global warming with breathtaking accuracy and warned executives of “potentially catastrophic” climate effects. 

Oil companies lied.

Starting in the late 1980s, oil companies spent the next two decades intentionally misleading the American public with a well-funded disinformation campaign intended to create doubt about climate science and generate mistrust in climate scientists.  

The result was a manufactured debate about climate change that undermined public understanding of the scientific consensus that climate change is real and human-caused. The fossil fuel industry’s internal memos made this propaganda strategy explicit: “Emphasize the uncertainty” in climate science and “Reposition global warming as theory (not fact).” Their goal was to confuse the public and policymakers in order to delay action and protect profits.

As part of this attack on the scientific consensus, oil companies issued statements and advertisements falsely claiming that climate science was “unsettled.” They also funded a small but vocal group of contrarian scientists and fake experts to sustain the illusion that there was significant disagreement within the scientific community. From 1986 to 2015, five oil companies alone spent $3.6 billion on advertising. Money also went to lobbying politicians against climate change legislation - outspending environmental groups by 10-to-1.

Oil companies harassed.

Climate scientists themselves also became the victims of an orchestrated smear campaign. For example, when one world-renowned climate scientist, Dr. Benjamin Santer, coauthored a major report concluding that human-caused global warming was underway, he was publicly accused of fraud and corruption by an oil-industry front group.Despite these claims being false and baseless, Dr. Santer faced harassment and threatening emails. 

When another prominent climate scientist, Dr. Michael Mann, coauthored research demonstrating rapid global warming over the past century, he was harassed for years by bogus legal complaints filed by organizations funded by fossil fuel interests. Fossil fuel companies used these attacks to misportray climate scientists as untrustworthy and convince the public not to believe their work.

When it comes to climate change, don’t trust the oil companies, trust the climate scientists.

By 1959–more than 60 years ago–they knew that burning fossil fuels could lead to global warming “sufficient to melt the icecap and submerge New York.” During the 1970s and ‘80s, scientists at one oil giant predicted global warming with breathtaking accuracy and warned executives of “potentially catastrophic” climate effects.

Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. income: $30,000 to $55,999.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Some people think that climate scientists cannot be trusted. You’d be forgiven for feeling that way, because the fossil fuel industry has bankrolled a multi-decade propaganda campaign specifically designed to stop action on climate change by undermining the public’s trust in climate science and scientists. Initially, in the 1970s and early 1980s, oil companies agreed with academic and federal scientists that burning fossil fuels would lead to climate change; some companies even employed their own climate scientists and conducted in-house climate science research. But as the public and politicians began to wake up to the climate crisis in the early 1990s, instead of alerting the public or taking action, the fossil fuel industry began to attack climate science and scientists. Trust the climate scientists, don’t let oil companies mislead you.

Here are some more details:

Oil companies knew.

Over the past decade, historians and journalists have discovered internal memos from oil companies showing that the oil industry has known since the 1950s that their products could cause dangerous climate change. Oil companies employed and worked with some of the world’s top climate scientists. By 1959–more than 60 years ago–they knew that burning fossil fuels could lead to global warming “sufficient to melt the icecap and submerge New York.” During the 1970s and ‘80s, scientists at one oil giant predicted global warming with breathtaking accuracy and warned executives of “potentially catastrophic” climate effects. 

Oil companies lied.

Starting in the late 1980s, oil companies spent the next two decades intentionally misleading the American public with a well-funded disinformation campaign intended to create doubt about climate science and generate mistrust in climate scientists.  

The result was a manufactured debate about climate change that undermined public understanding of the scientific consensus that climate change is real and human-caused. The fossil fuel industry’s internal memos made this propaganda strategy explicit: “Emphasize the uncertainty” in climate science and “Reposition global warming as theory (not fact).” Their goal was to confuse the public and policymakers in order to delay action and protect profits.

As part of this attack on the scientific consensus, oil companies issued statements and advertisements falsely claiming that climate science was “unsettled.” They also funded a small but vocal group of contrarian scientists and fake experts to sustain the illusion that there was significant disagreement within the scientific community. From 1986 to 2015, five oil companies alone spent $3.6 billion on advertising. Money also went to lobbying politicians against climate change legislation - outspending environmental groups by 10-to-1.

Oil companies harassed.

Climate scientists themselves also became the victims of an orchestrated smear campaign. For example, when one world-renowned climate scientist, Dr. Benjamin Santer, coauthored a major report concluding that human-caused global warming was underway, he was publicly accused of fraud and corruption by an oil-industry front group.Despite these claims being false and baseless, Dr. Santer faced harassment and threatening emails. 

When another prominent climate scientist, Dr. Michael Mann, coauthored research demonstrating rapid global warming over the past century, he was harassed for years by bogus legal complaints filed by organizations funded by fossil fuel interests. Fossil fuel companies used these attacks to misportray climate scientists as untrustworthy and convince the public not to believe their work.

When it comes to climate change, don’t trust the oil companies, trust the climate scientists.

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Some people think that climate scientists cannot be trusted. You’d be forgiven for feeling that way, because the fossil fuel industry has bankrolled a multi-decade propaganda campaign specifically designed to stop action on climate change by undermining the public’s trust in climate science and scientists. Initially, in the 1970s and early 1980s, oil companies agreed with academic and federal scientists that burning fossil fuels would lead to climate change; some companies even employed their own climate scientists and conducted in-house climate science research. But as the public and politicians began to wake up to the climate crisis in the early 1990s, instead of alerting the public or taking action, the fossil fuel industry began to attack climate science and scientists. Trust the climate scientists, don’t let oil companies mislead you.

Here are some more details:

Oil companies knew.

Over the past decade, historians and journalists have discovered internal memos from oil companies showing that the oil industry has known since the 1950s that their products could cause dangerous climate change. Oil companies employed and worked with some of the world’s top climate scientists. By 1959–more than 60 years ago–they knew that burning fossil fuels could lead to global warming “sufficient to melt the icecap and submerge New York.” During the 1970s and ‘80s, scientists at one oil giant predicted global warming with breathtaking accuracy and warned executives of “potentially catastrophic” climate effects. 

Oil companies lied.

Starting in the late 1980s, oil companies spent the next two decades intentionally misleading the American public with a well-funded disinformation campaign intended to create doubt about climate science and generate mistrust in climate scientists.  

The result was a manufactured debate about climate change that undermined public understanding of the scientific consensus that climate change is real and human-caused. The fossil fuel industry’s internal memos made this propaganda strategy explicit: “Emphasize the uncertainty” in climate science and “Reposition global warming as theory (not fact).” Their goal was to confuse the public and policymakers in order to delay action and protect profits.

As part of this attack on the scientific consensus, oil companies issued statements and advertisements falsely claiming that climate science was “unsettled.” They also funded a small but vocal group of contrarian scientists and fake experts to sustain the illusion that there was significant disagreement within the scientific community. From 1986 to 2015, five oil companies alone spent $3.6 billion on advertising. Money also went to lobbying politicians against climate change legislation - outspending environmental groups by 10-to-1.

Oil companies harassed.

Climate scientists themselves also became the victims of an orchestrated smear campaign. For example, when one world-renowned climate scientist, Dr. Benjamin Santer, coauthored a major report concluding that human-caused global warming was underway, he was publicly accused of fraud and corruption by an oil-industry front group.Despite these claims being false and baseless, Dr. Santer faced harassment and threatening emails. 

When another prominent climate scientist, Dr. Michael Mann, coauthored research demonstrating rapid global warming over the past century, he was harassed for years by bogus legal complaints filed by organizations funded by fossil fuel interests. Fossil fuel companies used these attacks to misportray climate scientists as untrustworthy and convince the public not to believe their work.

When it comes to climate change, don’t trust the oil companies, trust the climate scientists.

Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. party: Other.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Some people think that climate scientists cannot be trusted. You’d be forgiven for feeling that way, because the fossil fuel industry has bankrolled a multi-decade propaganda campaign specifically designed to stop action on climate change by undermining the public’s trust in climate science and scientists. Initially, in the 1970s and early 1980s, oil companies agreed with academic and federal scientists that burning fossil fuels would lead to climate change; some companies even employed their own climate scientists and conducted in-house climate science research. But as the public and politicians began to wake up to the climate crisis in the early 1990s, instead of alerting the public or taking action, the fossil fuel industry began to attack climate science and scientists. Trust the climate scientists, don’t let oil companies mislead you.

Here are some more details:

Oil companies knew.

Over the past decade, historians and journalists have discovered internal memos from oil companies showing that the oil industry has known since the 1950s that their products could cause dangerous climate change. Oil companies employed and worked with some of the world’s top climate scientists. By 1959–more than 60 years ago–they knew that burning fossil fuels could lead to global warming “sufficient to melt the icecap and submerge New York.” During the 1970s and ‘80s, scientists at one oil giant predicted global warming with breathtaking accuracy and warned executives of “potentially catastrophic” climate effects. 

Oil companies lied.

Starting in the late 1980s, oil companies spent the next two decades intentionally misleading the American public with a well-funded disinformation campaign intended to create doubt about climate science and generate mistrust in climate scientists.  

The result was a manufactured debate about climate change that undermined public understanding of the scientific consensus that climate change is real and human-caused. The fossil fuel industry’s internal memos made this propaganda strategy explicit: “Emphasize the uncertainty” in climate science and “Reposition global warming as theory (not fact).” Their goal was to confuse the public and policymakers in order to delay action and protect profits.

As part of this attack on the scientific consensus, oil companies issued statements and advertisements falsely claiming that climate science was “unsettled.” They also funded a small but vocal group of contrarian scientists and fake experts to sustain the illusion that there was significant disagreement within the scientific community. From 1986 to 2015, five oil companies alone spent $3.6 billion on advertising. Money also went to lobbying politicians against climate change legislation - outspending environmental groups by 10-to-1.

Oil companies harassed.

Climate scientists themselves also became the victims of an orchestrated smear campaign. For example, when one world-renowned climate scientist, Dr. Benjamin Santer, coauthored a major report concluding that human-caused global warming was underway, he was publicly accused of fraud and corruption by an oil-industry front group.Despite these claims being false and baseless, Dr. Santer faced harassment and threatening emails. 

When another prominent climate scientist, Dr. Michael Mann, coauthored research demonstrating rapid global warming over the past century, he was harassed for years by bogus legal complaints filed by organizations funded by fossil fuel interests. Fossil fuel companies used these attacks to misportray climate scientists as untrustworthy and convince the public not to believe their work.

When it comes to climate change, don’t trust the oil companies, trust the climate scientists.

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Some people think that climate scientists cannot be trusted. You’d be forgiven for feeling that way, because the fossil fuel industry has bankrolled a multi-decade propaganda campaign specifically designed to stop action on climate change by undermining the public’s trust in climate science and scientists. Initially, in the 1970s and early 1980s, oil companies agreed with academic and federal scientists that burning fossil fuels would lead to climate change; some companies even employed their own climate scientists and conducted in-house climate science research. But as the public and politicians began to wake up to the climate crisis in the early 1990s, instead of alerting the public or taking action, the fossil fuel industry began to attack climate science and scientists. Trust the climate scientists, don’t let oil companies mislead you.

Here are some more details:

Oil companies knew.

Over the past decade, historians and journalists have discovered internal memos from oil companies showing that the oil industry has known since the 1950s that their products could cause dangerous climate change. Oil companies employed and worked with some of the world’s top climate scientists. By 1959–more than 60 years ago–they knew that burning fossil fuels could lead to global warming “sufficient to melt the icecap and submerge New York.” During the 1970s and ‘80s, scientists at one oil giant predicted global warming with breathtaking accuracy and warned executives of “potentially catastrophic” climate effects. 

Oil companies lied.

Starting in the late 1980s, oil companies spent the next two decades intentionally misleading the American public with a well-funded disinformation campaign intended to create doubt about climate science and generate mistrust in climate scientists.  

The result was a manufactured debate about climate change that undermined public understanding of the scientific consensus that climate change is real and human-caused. The fossil fuel industry’s internal memos made this propaganda strategy explicit: “Emphasize the uncertainty” in climate science and “Reposition global warming as theory (not fact).” Their goal was to confuse the public and policymakers in order to delay action and protect profits.

As part of this attack on the scientific consensus, oil companies issued statements and advertisements falsely claiming that climate science was “unsettled.” They also funded a small but vocal group of contrarian scientists and fake experts to sustain the illusion that there was significant disagreement within the scientific community. From 1986 to 2015, five oil companies alone spent $3.6 billion on advertising. Money also went to lobbying politicians against climate change legislation - outspending environmental groups by 10-to-1.

Oil companies harassed.

Climate scientists themselves also became the victims of an orchestrated smear campaign. For example, when one world-renowned climate scientist, Dr. Benjamin Santer, coauthored a major report concluding that human-caused global warming was underway, he was publicly accused of fraud and corruption by an oil-industry front group.Despite these claims being false and baseless, Dr. Santer faced harassment and threatening emails. 

When another prominent climate scientist, Dr. Michael Mann, coauthored research demonstrating rapid global warming over the past century, he was harassed for years by bogus legal complaints filed by organizations funded by fossil fuel interests. Fossil fuel companies used these attacks to misportray climate scientists as untrustworthy and convince the public not to believe their work.

When it comes to climate change, don’t trust the oil companies, trust the climate scientists.
